blocks.p: It made him the offer on the second night, in the small hours, in the one place he had not expected. His own kitchen. The cold kettle, the table, the chair. Everything was set exactly as it had been on the morning this began. Outside, the street was silent except for the drip of an air conditioner onto a tin roof below the window. The Healer had spent a month inside Gin's memories. It knew exactly which room would do the most work for it.

Gin sat across from him in his own body. The calm in him was complete and gentle. That calm was how Rei always knew the Healer was the one speaking. It laid the offer out the way it laid everything out, item by item, and every item was true. Rei could not argue with any of it, because each line was real. "You found the Axis," it said, almost tenderly. "Then you know there must be a thirteenth. You know the wound will not close by itself. And you know Kishin will tear it open whether I take the chair or not. So let me make you an honest offer. The first one anyone has made you since this kitchen."

Then it did the thing Rei had not seen coming, the thing that turned the whole month inside out. It offered the chair to him. Not as a threat. Not as a trap he could name. As mercy, item by item. "The seat is not particular about who fills it," it said. "It wants only to be filled by something that can hold the difference. I am built for it. But you, Rei. Two paths, held down your whole life precisely because they were strong enough to need holding down. You could hold it too. Take the Thirteenth Domain yourself, and the wound closes around you instead of me. Your brother is set down whole the moment it does, because I will no longer need him. You would stop being a witness with no grade. You would become the law the whole registered world has scrambled to stand in for. You would have saved the district, and saved Gin. And the only cost is the one thing you have spent your life refusing to pick up."

It was the most reasonable offer anyone had ever made him, and it was built entirely out of true things. Rei sat in the chair from that first morning and felt how easily a person could drown in it. Because it was not lying. He probably could take the seat. The wall probably would close. Gin probably would be set down whole. And there was one thing it did not list, because it did not need to. It knew he could already feel it. That thing was what happened to the person who held the seat.

There was no climbing back down from a Domain. Rei had seen the man at the hub. The weight was permanent and total, and it was not human. Rei would save his brother by becoming a pressure with a name Gin almost knew. A law instead of a brother. A pair of eyes in a dark room, which Gin could feel but could never again sit across a kitchen table from. The Healer was offering him everyone's life but his own. It offered gently, and it meant it, and that was the worst part. The kindest way out of all this was the one where Rei stopped, forever, being someone Gin could come home to.

Gin surfaced while the offer was still warm on the table. The real Gin, coming up through the calm for about as long as a person can hold his breath. Rei knew him at once. The mercy went out of the eyes, and what came up behind it was tired and frightened and completely Gin. He could not stay long. He spent what he had on the only things that mattered, fast, the way a man speaks under water.

"Don't take it," he said. His hand found the edge of the table, the same way it had once found the phone receiver, and tapped. Once, then once, then once. It was the knock from the widow's altar, the knock from the inside. In the code he had taught Rei, it meant this was true, and not the Healer wearing truth like a coat. "It's not lying to you. That's how I know not to let you say yes. It would do it. It would set me down. And I would have to live in a city you became the underside of."

Then he tried to tell Rei the thing he had been tapping toward since the first time he broke through, the thing the Healer would not let him finish in words. He got most of it out in broken half sentences, like a man coming up between waves. When the Healer took him, it had not taken an empty man. It had taken a man who had spent his whole career writing names small in the back of a book. A man who had held wards by committee and done the plain, heavy work of keeping the wall shut, one favour at a time. And at some point in a month of being worn, he had come to understand the chair from inside the very thing that wanted it. There was a way to deny the chair to both demons. He had not been allowed to say it aloud, and even now, with the leash this tight, he could not. He could only give Rei the edge of it.

"The chair doesn't need a new occupant," he managed. "It needs its old one. The torn-out thing isn't gone, Rei. It was put somewhere. I helped put it. We all did, the whole registered world, that's what the wards are..."

Then the leash pulled, the way a captor's leash always pulls hardest the moment the captive sees it. The calm came back into the eyes like water closing over a swimmer, and Gin was gone again in the middle of a word. The Healer sat across from Rei in his brother's body, with its gentle, terrible patience. It had heard every syllable. Now it knew exactly how much Gin understood, and exactly how much he had managed to give away before the wave took him.

Rei sat with three knocks fading on the table, a half sentence, and the nights running out. His brother had just spent what might be his last clear strength. He had not spent it on being saved. He had spent it on handing Rei the one thing the Axis had not shown him. The wound had an old occupant. And Rei had seen him. A man at the hub with his back to the world, who had sat in the Duty chair first and never fully stood up. It was a person once. The archive notes say so.

The whole registered world had put him somewhere. It had put him inside a name. The Architect. A mechanism. Register XIII, null-emotive. Every ward in the city leaned its weight on him and called him a law of nature, so that nobody would have to remember he had been a man. That was the lock. And the only one who could tell Rei how to open it was the man himself. He answered one question each time someone reached him, and only to those who came all the way in.

On the third afternoon of Obon, Rei walked down the slope to Ōji. The heat was over thirty-four degrees, and the air was so wet it felt like walking through a towel. The cicadas in the trees of Asukayama park were screaming, thousands of them, a sound so loud and steady that after a minute he stopped hearing it, the way he would stop hearing a fridge. In August the park was only green and loud, and the shade under its trees was the only cool place for streets around.

At the bottom of the slope, the little Toden tram came grinding round the corner. It rang its bell at a man on a bicycle. Through its window Rei saw an old couple sitting very straight, holding a paper bag of offerings between them. Incense, a box of sweets, a bunch of yellow chrysanthemums. They were going to a family grave. Half of Tokyo was going to a family grave this week. The city was emptier than usual, because so many people had gone back to their home towns for the festival, and the ones left behind moved slowly in the heat.

The station was busy anyway. Ōji is where the sky-blue trains of the Keihin-Tōhoku line stop above the street, and where the Namboku subway line runs underneath. The ticket gates beeped as people tapped their Suica cards. A station jingle played, a short bright tune, and a train pulled out overhead with a long sigh of brakes. A schoolgirl in a summer uniform stood by the exit fanning herself with a paper fan from some shop, her eyes shut. A salaryman in a white shirt drank a whole can of cold tea from the vending machine in one go and put the empty can in the bin without looking at it. Nobody looked up at the grey building across the road.

The CVD building was a grey block one minute from the east exit of Ōji station. It had been built on the thinnest point of the ward on purpose. Rei walked into it with paper lanterns still sagging over the intake desk from the start of the festival. Okada Shizuka came down to the lobby herself. She looked at his face, then at his hands, the way she always did.
"Gin told me to watch for you," she said. "I've been watching. Come on."

He told her in the lift, as plainly as he could. The Axis. The man at the hub. Gin's half sentence. He needed to go through to the other side with his body, and come back. And he needed a door that the Healer's rats could not follow and the Division's instruments could not read. Okada listened with her three notebooks pressed to her chest and did not interrupt. When the doors opened on the third level underground, she did not step out at once.
"I'll show you what there is," she said. "Then you choose. I won't choose for you."

She walked him the long way. Later he understood that she had wanted him to see it. They passed a wide window onto the Training Hall. There were mats on the floor and protective lines burned black into the boards. At the far end, a weak spirit was held on a tether, a patch of cold that the new trainees took turns practising their reading on. The trainees were young. Most of them were seventeen. One said something and the others burst out laughing, the loud kind of laughter frightened people use to cover their fear. An instructor told them to settle down without much force. "They teach the half that keeps the institution comfortable," Okada said. "Your brother used to say that. He wrote the other half down."

They passed the Sigil Room. This was where the CVD's masters drew protective glyphs onto paper, and onto skin. Rei smelled it before he saw it. Sumi, the black ink of calligraphy, and blood. There were long benches and the hands of masters, and the only sound was the scratch of brushes on washi, the thin handmade paper used for seals. At the back of the room, a curtain hung across a single bench. "That's where they make an operative into someone the registry can't read," Okada said, quietly. "You don't watch them work, and you don't choose the artist. Gin learned his own keying so he'd never have to sit there again." She kept walking.

blocks.cap: The Mirror Room, which never closes

blocks.p: There was a door with no window and a Surveillance seal. Behind it was a faint sound, like birds in a tree far away. "The Mirror Room," Okada said, without slowing down. "I told you about it once. Now you know what the mirrors are bound to. Every one of them a crow somebody fed for three days." She did not look at the door. "It never closes." She tilted her head at the next door along, which had a number on it and nothing else. "And that one is Special Cases. That's where the possession that should not work goes, and the operative who came back wrong. They study them gently and everyone calls it care." Then she stopped and looked at him. "Ask me how many people have gone where you want to go. Then ask me how many came back right. Most of the ones who came back at all came back wrong, Rei. Some of them are very calm about it. One of them gardens. It's in the file."
Rei did not answer. She nodded as if he had, and opened a door at the end of the corridor. It should have opened onto a stairwell.

blocks.cap: The walled green three floors underground

blocks.p: It opened onto grass. A walled green field under an open sky, which was impossible, three floors underground. In the middle was a sparring circle worn down to bare dirt. At the far end, where the instructors could see and the new trainees could not, two mediums were fighting for real. One of them was on her knees and getting up again. "Channel rank and above for that," Okada said. "Forms for everybody else. You leave here knowing what your ability does when a hand is genuinely trying to end you." Along one wall stood an aviary full of noisy, squabbling crows. On a perch at its end sat a falcon with its hood pushed back off its head. It turned its eyes on Rei and held them. He had the clear feeling of being seen on both sides of the wall at once. "It can see the veil," Okada said. "Trained. It frightened your brother more than the sparring did."

blocks.cap: The cattery, five cats on five cushions

blocks.p: The last door was warm. The room behind it smelled of clean straw and old paper. Five cats lay on five cushions, each with a small brass tag. Sera. Itou. Mochida. Hara. Kuga. "Names of five operatives who didn't come back," Okada said quietly. "The handler named the cats for them." The senior handler was a woman who did not give her name and did not look up from the cat in her lap. Kuga lay on the cushion by the window. He was a big grey cat with torn ears, and he did not look up either.
Okada sat Rei down on a wooden crate and explained.

"There are two ways for someone like you to put his body through and get it back," she said. "The first is the False Death. Pufferfish toxin and snake venom, mixed to a ratio the archive keeps. Forty-eight hours to prepare it, no less. The person going under needs Psychometabolism at the third level, and a second person with it at the second level has to sit the watch and run the return. You hold an object against your breastbone, something you've carried more than a year, so your soul can find the body again. Three to seven minutes and you have no pulse. To anything below Class A you read as dead. Your consciousness waits at the Threshold. The window to bring you back is three or four hours. Nobody has come back after eight." She paused. "There's one death on record from doing it without a monitor. And the Threshold is not empty. Things there can reach a soul held that close to the door."
"I don't have Psychometabolism," Rei said. "And I don't have forty-eight hours."

"No." She looked at the cushion by the window. "The second way is a cat. Still water at least two centimetres deep, still enough to be a mirror. You stand in it barefoot. You hold the cat against your chest with both hands. You look into its eyes and you do not look away. Rank doesn't come into it. The cat's pupil is the aperture. If it consents, and it takes ten seconds to forty for it to decide, its weight changes in your hands and the room behind it stops being the room. That's the door. Your sight goes up a tier. You can step partway through, or with a cat that knows the way, much further. The cat chooses the distance. Not you. It costs you eight points of stability to open. It holds fifteen to thirty minutes. Nobody has held one past forty. When the cat looks away, the door shuts, at once, with no warning." She turned back to him. "To our instruments you'll read as a stray cat and nothing else. That's why it's the cleanest crossing there is. But it doesn't make you invisible to anything already on the other side. Know the difference."

"I cross through Kuga and no other when it truly matters," the handler said, still without looking up. "But he's not mine to lend. Access is the handler and the cat's consent. The cat's consent outranks me."

blocks.cap: Kuga, the grey cat with the torn ears

blocks.p: Kuga opened his eyes. He got down off his cushion without hurry, the way cats do everything. He crossed the straw and sat at Rei's feet. Then he looked up into Rei's face and kept looking.
The handler let out a breath. "Well," she said. "That's that, then."

Okada signed the cat out on a clipboard by the door, under her own name. Rei watched her do it. He knew exactly which rule she was breaking, and how much she would hate herself for it later. She did not say anything about it. She only said, "The node behind the Senju waterworks. Gin marked it smallest. The smallest tear is the one most likely to let a living man back out. I'll meet you there after dark with the water."

Rei carried Kuga out through the east exit in a plastic carrier with a grille at the front. The cat did not make a sound. On the platform above, a train came in and the doors opened and a crowd of tired people came down the stairs with suitcases, back from their home towns, already sunburned. A small boy pressed his face to the grille of the carrier and said "Neko!", the word for cat, and his mother pulled him away with an apology. Rei bowed to her a little. He did not trust himself to speak.

By the time he reached the seam in Kita, the sun was down. The third night came the way the bottom of a held breath comes. He stood on the embankment with the carrier at his feet. Below him, in the old streets, the first sending-fires were being lit, early, the way Kita lit everything early now. Okuribi. Small flames in clay dishes by the front doors, to guide the dead gently back to the other side. Each one was a family's tenderness. And each one, this year, was a small part of the pull the Healer had spent a month preparing to borrow. He could feel the turning point through his two open paths. The great seasonal lean of the world was beginning to swing, from welcome to farewell. At the peak of each small swing, the curtain over the wound went from thin to almost nothing. He could feel how it would be on the last night, when the swing was complete and the door stood open both ways at once.

Kishin was already leaning into the gap, hunger turned into weather, its mouth somewhere in the dark below with Kaito's young face. The Healer was already climbing. Gin's body was carrying it toward the place where the chair would be, calm as a man keeping an appointment. And Rei stood between them at the wound, with everything he had learned and no law of his own. The structure waited for him to choose which fire the night would light. It had been patient since before the wards had names.

Standing there with the okuribi burning below him, he understood that this had never been a puzzle with a solution. There was no move that saved everything. The Axis had shown him that, and the offer in the kitchen had proved it. Every way off this embankment cost something. He could trust the monster in his brother's body and bet the district on its mercy. He could throw himself against the wound and hope his mind lasted longer than the night. He could take Gin's hand and walk away and let the lanterns go out over a ward that had lit them early. He could feel each choice the way he could feel the slope, and none of them was clean. Only one thing in the whole structure was not already decided. It was the half sentence his brother had drowned to give him. It needs its old one.

The sending-fires burned. The hinge of the year swung. His brother climbed toward the chair, and somewhere under the calm, a held breath of his own was still knocking. Once, then once, then once. Whatever Rei chose, he would choose for all of it. The wall, the district, the chair, the man. And for the person he would be on the far side of this, who was not the person who had stood in a cold kitchen a few nights ago, a whole life ago, and counted the doors the morning had left open. The structure would not decide for him. The demons could not. And Gin, drowned and knocking, had spent everything he had to leave it in Rei's hands.

Rei breathed in the warm air the city was letting go of. He did not choose the fire yet. He chose the door. Before he chose anything for all of it, he would go down and ask the old occupant the one question he was allowed. He picked up the carrier. Kuga shifted inside it. And Rei went down off the seam, toward the river and the waterworks, where Okada was waiting with the water.
